title: Why the Omer mourns (Yevamot 62b)
hook: the Talmud says Akiva's students died in these weeks for not honoring each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lag BaOmer, bonfires and Rabbi Shimon. Your line was a break in the sadness. Today, the sadness itself: why these weeks mourn at all.

Twelve thousand pairs of students. That's the number the Talmud gives for the disciples of Rabbi Akiva, spread across the land from Gevat to Antipatris. A whole generation of learners, studying in pairs, arguing over the words of the Torah. If any group seemed set to carry the tradition forward, it was this one. And according to the Talmud, in a single season, all of them died. Its explanation isn't war, or a lack of learning. It's how they treated each other.
screen: `A WHOLE GENERATION OF LEARNERS.` → `GONE IN ONE SEASON.` → `HOW THEY TREATED EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: The passage is in tractate Yevamot, page 62b. Twelve thousand pairs means twenty-four thousand students, and all of them died in one period, because they did not treat each other with respect. They died, it adds, between Passover and Shavuot, and the world was desolate. Then Akiva went south and taught just five new students, among them Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, from yesterday. Those five carried the Torah forward. Now the irony. Rabbi Akiva is the one who called a verse from Leviticus, in the old Jewish translation, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," a great principle of the Torah. In the Talmud's account, his own students fell short of that very teaching. They knew the texts; they didn't honor the people learning beside them. Some historians suggest the deaths may also reflect the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome, in which Akiva supported the rebels; the Talmud doesn't say so. Either way, the rabbis chose to remember it as a lesson about respect. That's why, in many communities, these weeks carry quiet mourning for part of the Omer: no weddings, no haircuts, no live music. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently. And some teachers turn the mourning into a task: if the students died for lack of honoring each other, the repair is to honor each other more, especially the people you argue with.
screen: `TWELVE THOUSAND PAIRS.` · `NO RESPECT FOR EACH OTHER.` · `FIVE STUDENTS IN THE SOUTH.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR, AKIVA TAUGHT.` · then, large: `HONOR EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you work, study or live beside, especially someone you disagree with, compete with, or take for granted, and picture their face. Name one thing about them that deserves honor, their effort, their honesty, their patience, a skill you don't have, and hold it until it feels true.
Rabbi Akiva, whose twenty-four thousand students all died in one season, the Talmud says, because they did not treat each other with respect.
Your line: honor each other. A week of enough, as if you left, an open door, a song of songs, one quality, a break in the sadness, and now honor. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.

howItsDone: During part of the Omer period, many Jews refrain from weddings, haircuts and live music in mourning for Rabbi Akiva's students; Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities count the mourning days differently, and many lift the customs on Lag BaOmer.

chat.says: Why do some Jews skip weddings and haircuts between Passover and Shavuot?
options: They mourn Rabbi Akiva's students, who died, the Talmud says, for lack of respect.
The Torah forbids celebrating until the barley harvest is fully gathered.
They mourn the Temple, which the Romans burned during the Omer weeks.
